combined with an almost entirely mandatory text and the boilerplate quahty 
of the disclaimer—was enough to peg the document as a legislative rule. But 
later, in National Mining Association v. McCarthy, 758 F.3d 243 (D.C. Cir. 
2014), the D.C. Circuit distinguished the document at issue (on criteria for 
obtaining certain permits) from the one in Appalachian Power on the ground 
that “the caveats [against binding status] run throughout the document, and 
more to the point, the document is devoid of relevant commands.” The court 
sided with the agency even while conceding that “regulated parties may feel 
pressure to voluntarily conform their behavior because the writing is on the 
wall about what will be needed to obtain a permit.” The court found this 
pressure legally unobjectionable because the agency, under Pacific Gas, still 
had to ‘he prepared to support the policy just as if the policy statement had 
never been issued.” The pattern of near-universal comphance invoked in 
Appalachian Power appears not to have been a factor in subsequent D.C. 
Circuit cases on this question.

F.3d at 34 (holding that an EPA memo’s establishment of a rebuttable 
presumption was not enough to render it a legislative rule).
The following case concerns the Department of Homeland Security’s 
(DHS) issuance of one of the most controversial guidance documents in 
recent decades. Understanding the controversy requires a bit of 
background. Milhons of people hving the United States do not have lawful 
immigration status and could lawfully be removed. But DHS’s hmited

congressional appropriations mean that it is practically capable of 
removing only a fraction of these people. Thus, DHS officials must 
inevitably exercise some sort of enforcement discretion, either consciously 
or imphcitly. At any given time, milhons of people lacking lawful 
immigration status are benefiting from that discretion, in that DHS is not 
trying to remove them.
